lens: Executive Product Design and Council Chair
method: Independent lens review of captured evidence. The director opened every screenshot for a surface before scoring it, read the axe and capture results, and scored without sight of any other director's scores.
overallNote:
Reviewed all fourteen captures plus both automated sets. The machine floor is clean: no axe violations on any surface at either viewport, no console errors, all 200s — that is a real and uncommon result, and it means every finding below is a judgement about craft, not a bug report.

Through the end-to-end lens, the product's strongest asset by a distance is its voice. The board's column explainers, 'Write the thought before it disappears…', 'Private to you', 'Live since 15 Jul 2026. Anyone holding the link can read it.', and 'Terms repeated before purchase' are all written by someone with a point of view, and they hold a consistent register across app and marketing. The second real asset is the Notes-to-Tasks spine: a task detail that names its source note, and a note footer that links forward to the task it became. That round-trip is the strongest evidence that these are one product rather than three sharing a nav.

Where it does not yet hang together is at the seams. The same data speaks different dialects depending on where you stand: the board shows a 'Mara & Finn' tag styled exactly like an assignee while the list says every one of the thirteen tasks is owned by Orla; identical empty conditions get two different sentences ('Nothing held up' vs 'No tasks in this group'); dates are relative in one view and absolute in another. Mobile repeatedly loses information the desktop had — Notes tab counts, the sort control, Timeline's whole-arc shape — rather than being redesigned for the smaller canvas. And the three marketing pages start their content column at three different left margins, which says there is no shared page grid underneath them.

Two findings are the load-bearing ones. In the app, the List view clips its priority column mid-word at standard desktop width, so the execution product truncates data in its default state. On marketing, the pricing page spends an entire desktop viewport on two display headlines without showing a single number — the highest-stakes page deferring its only job below the fold.

No vetoes. Nothing here would embarrass the company or block a user outright, and the 'In development. You're seeing it early.' toast is honest signposting for a pre-release baseline rather than a defect, though it does obscure content in six of the ten app captures. I have given no credit for what static captures cannot show — motion, real assistive-technology behaviour, performance under load, or any mutation path (drag, save, share, checkout) that these stills do not exercise. Every score assumes those are unproven. Nothing reaches the 9.5 release floor; the range is genuinely good, considered work with real and specific gaps, with pricing the one surface I would call visibly unfinished.

surfaces.rationale: The board is the considered half: column counts plus one-line plain-English explainers ('Agreed and ready to start.', 'Held by a reply, a delivery, or a decision.') do real first-contact work, and the Waiting empty state reads 'Nothing held up'. The List view is where the product stops hanging together. At 1440px the table overflows: the fifth column header is clipped to 'P' and its values render as 'Hig', 'Low', 'No' cut mid-word against the right edge — priority is unreadable in the default desktop state. Every list row carries two near-identical circular controls (selection checkbox and status toggle) with only one labelled header. Status is stated three times per row: group header, status pill, and circle. Most damaging across views, OWNER reads 'Orla' on all thirteen rows while the board surfaces only 'Mara & Finn' chips styled identically to category chips ('Venue', 'Bar', 'Enquiry') — so the board shows a tag where a reader will assume an assignee, and never shows the actual owner. The same empty condition speaks in two voices ('Nothing held up' on board, 'No tasks in this group' in list), and dates shift vocabulary between views ('Due today' / 'Overdue by 2 days' vs 'Due 16 Jul' / 'Due 14 Jul'). Done cards carry green tinted fills that make finished work the loudest thing on the board. Mobile stacks six rows of chrome before the first card and ships two view switchers at once — the Board/List/Schedule/Calendar tabs and a 'Board' selector in the bottom nav.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Make the two views agree: fit the List table to a 1440px viewport so priority is never clipped mid-word, and give the board card a distinct assignee treatment showing the real owner (Orla) separate from tag chips, so a board reader and a list reader draw the same conclusion about who holds the work.

surfaces.rationale: The best-constructed surface in the app. The action row groups status, assignee with a '+' affordance, due date, priority and a single dominant 'Mark done' primary — one obvious next move. Empty states do explanatory work rather than apologising ('No conversation yet. Comments and changes will appear here as they happen.'), the resource dropzone states both paths ('Drop files here, or paste a link…'), and the keyboard hint teaches progressively. The 'SOURCE — From Notes' field is the strongest structural idea in the product: it makes the Notes-to-Tasks spine visible at the record level and round-trips to the link I later saw in the Notes footer. Gaps are all in the metadata rail. 'From Notes · open source' collides with a loaded term of art and reads as a licensing claim rather than 'open the source note'. Below it an unlabelled paragraph — 'Approved wording: "Confirm marquee sides with hire company before Thursday"' — floats as body copy among labelled fields, and differs from the task title ('with the hire company'), raising a question of which is authoritative without answering it. 'COPIES / Make copies' names no concept a newcomer holds, and 'ADD FIELD / + Amount' offers a single field type phrased as a noun. 'DRAFT A REPLY' is set in uppercase against sentence-case buttons everywhere else. On mobile the rail order is inherited rather than rethought: repeats, tags, contact and project sit below the entire conversation block, so the most consultable facts are the last thing reachable.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Reorder the mobile layout so the metadata rail (repeats, tags, contact, project, source) sits directly under the description rather than below the conversation, and relabel 'open source' and 'Make copies' to name what they actually do.

surfaces.rationale: The most complete product story in the set. The composer prompt — 'Write the thought before it disappears…' — states the product's reason for existing in six words, and Type/Voice/Photo makes capture modality a first-class choice rather than a settings toggle. The triage model is legible without instruction: Notebook 14 / Review 8 / In Tasks 6, with 'To review' items revealing Keep / Turn into task / Delete inline at the item, decisions offered where the decision is. Per-row modality icons (document, microphone, image) mean you can see how a thought arrived at a glance. 'Private to you' with a lock sits in the header as a standing trust statement. The detail footer closes the loop — 'Captured 35 minutes ago / Edited 31 minutes ago' plus 'In Tasks — Confirm marquee sides with hire company before Thursday' as a live link back to the task I opened separately. That round-trip is the single best evidence that these are one product and not three. Against that: the detail pane leaves roughly 350px of empty white between a three-line note and its footer, and short notes are the common case for a capture tool, so the default impression is unfinished rather than airy. 'Save note' — the primary action of a capture product — is the quietest button on screen, a low-emphasis outline. The header says 'Written' where the footer says 'Captured' for the same event on the same pane. Mobile silently drops the tab counts (14/8/6), which are the whole triage signal, and the 'Newest first' sort control disappears rather than relocating.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Fix the reading pane for short notes — anchor the metadata footer directly under the body instead of to the bottom of the viewport — and promote 'Save note' to a filled primary so the capture product's core action is its most confident button.

surfaces.rationale: The most distinctive surface and the one that most looks like a designed artifact rather than a CRUD screen: 'Mara & Finn' at display scale, a restrained single violet accent, a '79 days' countdown with '2 of 9 complete', and an axis with month ticks and milestones alternating above and below. 'Live since 15 Jul 2026. Anyone holding the link can read it.' is the best sentence in the entire review set — it states the sharing state and its exact consequence in plain language, and the Preview control alongside Share lets an owner check what a recipient sees. The '4 milestones' bracket is a real answer to label collision rather than letting nodes overlap. But the emphasis is inverted for a direction surface. The completed Jan-to-Apr span renders as a thick black line with two generously labelled milestones across half the width, while the near future compresses seven nodes into the right quarter behind an unlabelled '4 milestones' bracket — the region that actually governs decisions is the least legible. The 'Today' marker is a plain grey tick, visually weaker than the month ticks beside it. The countdown appears twice on one screen in two formats ('79 days to go' in the header, '79 / days' in the hero). At 1440x900 the fold cuts through the 'Menu tasting at The Orchard' detail headline. On mobile the axis becomes a vertical dot-and-rule list: a reasonable adaptation, but the whole-arc-at-a-glance idea that justifies this surface does not survive, and nothing replaces it — on the device most likely to open a shared link. Static captures cannot show whatever motion carries this page, and I have scored it without credit for that.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Rebalance the axis so the near future gets the space the completed past currently holds — label the four clustered milestones inline and make 'Today' the strongest mark on the line.

surfaces.rationale: The positioning is sharp and the copy is the site's real asset: 'Project management for people outside tech.' with 'outside' carrying the one violet accent, and a subhead that lands the whole thesis — 'One calm system for people with work to manage, not software to manage.' The 'NOTES → TASKS → TIMELINE' mono line states the spine before any feature does. Two well-differentiated CTAs. What undercuts it is that a full desktop viewport of a design-led product's front door contains no product. 'See the system at work' is a promise the fold does not keep — there is no screenshot, no frame, no fragment of the interface above 900px, only type. For a company whose pitch is that the thing feels considered, showing none of it in the first screen argues against itself. Composition compounds it: the CTAs finish around y=612 and the hero runs on to a section rule near y=838, leaving roughly 200px of dead band with the 'NOTES → TASKS → TIMELINE' line floating alone in it. The hero content column starts at x=280 while the header logo sits at x=124, and nothing else on the page establishes that 280 grid — it reads as drift rather than intent, and the other two marketing pages use two further different left margins. Mobile is the better-composed of the two: the headline wraps to four lines cleanly, CTAs stack full-width, and the narrative section 'ONE THREAD, THROUGH THE STUDIO / Follow one wedding' begins within the first scroll. Mobile also carries two competing nav affordances, an exposed 'Products' dropdown beside a hamburger.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Put real product into the first desktop screen — a live Timeline or board frame beside the headline — so 'See the system at work' is answered at the fold, and align the hero's left edge to the header grid.

surfaces.rationale: The writing here is the best on the site and it is doing genuine strategic work: 'Project management software was built by tech companies, for tech companies' followed by a paragraph that concedes before it argues — 'Sprints, epics, backlogs, story points, stand-ups and retrospectives can all be useful when the work calls for them.' That is confident, non-defensive positioning, and the mobile pull line 'The mistake was assuming every project should work that way.' lands the turn. The thin left rule descending from a violet dot under 'A NOTE FROM THE FOUNDER', with circular nodes marking later sections, is a proper editorial spine and the most systematic device on the marketing site. The desktop composition wastes the canvas it asked for. The headline is set hard-left at x=124 while the body paragraph is dropped into a right column at x=732, leaving roughly 600x240px of dead space at bottom-left with the vertical rule running through nothing. The eye has to jump 600px to find the argument, and the fold arrives before the pull line — so the mobile version, in a single well-set column, delivers more of the case in its first screen than the desktop does in a canvas three times wider. And a founder's note names no founder in its opening screen: no signature, no name, no face where the page's entire job is establishing who stands behind this. The eyebrow is set in black caps here, violet mono on Pricing, grey mono on Landing — three treatments of one element across three pages.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Rework the desktop composition to fill the dead lower-left quadrant — bring the body column back under the headline and pull the 'The mistake was assuming…' line above the fold — and sign the note with the founder's name.

surfaces.rationale: This is the page where a real person decides whether to trust the product with money, and a full 1440x900 desktop screen of it contains no price. The viewport holds a display hero ('One clear system. Four ways in.'), a subhead, a reassurance strip, and then a second display hero ('Choose by the work in front of you.') — two stacked heroes and roughly 300px of combined empty band before any plan, number, or comparison appears. The one question a visitor arrives with goes unanswered until they scroll past the fold. The reassurance strip is good, honest content — 'No charge on the waitlist', 'VAT included at the prevailing rate', 'Terms repeated before purchase' is a genuinely trustworthy promise and EU-aware — but it reassures about a price that has not yet been shown. The copy also reads provisional where it must read settled: 'the terms settled today' and 'Anything unresolved is named plainly' tell a buyer that some of this is still moving. 'or shape an Enterprise start with Ethan' introduces a first name with no prior context on this page — charming to someone who has read the About page, opaque to the enterprise buyer it is aimed at, who is the audience least tolerant of it. The content column starts at x=160 against a header logo at x=124, and this is the third distinct left margin across three marketing pages (Landing 280, About 124, Pricing 160) — across a three-page site there is no shared page grid. Mobile compresses the same order more forgivably, but still shows no number in its first screen.
surfaces.highestLeverageFix: Get a price into the first desktop screen — collapse the two stacked heroes into one and lift the plan comparison above the fold, with the reassurance strip following the numbers it reassures about rather than preceding them.
